title: To-Infinitives and Preposition + -ing
summary: Choose between adjective + to-infinitive and adjective + preposition + -ing according to meaning. Distinguish fear of taking an action from fear of an outcome, interest in a possible activity from a reaction to news, and an apology for a past act from regret or a polite interruption.
learningObjectives: Distinguish afraid to do (hesitation about an action) from afraid of doing (fear of a possible result).
Use interested in + -ing for considering an activity and interested to hear, see or know for a reaction or enquiry.
Choose sorry for + -ing to apologise for actions and sorry to + infinitive for a reaction or a polite interruption.
Select to-infinitives or preposition + -ing after common verbs including plan, prevent, insist, succeed and look forward.

explanation.heading: Afraid to act versus afraid of an outcome
explanation.body: Afraid to + base verb often means a person does not want to take an action because it feels risky or uncomfortable. Afraid of + -ing expresses worry that an event may occur, often unintentionally. The two can work together: afraid to approach an animal because afraid of being scratched. Context matters; these are useful typical contrasts rather than rigid rules for every possible sentence.
explanation.example: Owen was afraid to open the gate because he was afraid of disturbing the dog.

explanation.heading: Interested in doing versus interested to hear
explanation.body: Interested in + -ing indicates curiosity about or willingness to take part in an activity: interested in joining a workshop. Interested to hear, see, learn or know presents a reaction to information or interest in receiving it; the latter is especially natural for announcements or discoveries. Do not replace in joining with to join in the standard interested-in-activity pattern.
explanation.example: We are interested in renting the studio, and we would be interested to know the monthly price.

explanation.heading: Sorry for doing versus sorry to do
explanation.body: Sorry for + -ing usually apologises for an action, often one already done: sorry for speaking sharply. Sorry to hear, learn, see or leave often expresses regret about a situation or news, not an admission of having caused it. Sorry to interrupt or sorry to bother you is also used when politely doing the action at that moment.
explanation.example: I am sorry for arriving late, and I am sorry to hear that you missed the show.

explanation.heading: After a verb, look for its required pattern
explanation.body: Several verbs are followed by a to-infinitive: want to leave, intend to apply, hope to win, promise to help and allow someone to enter. Other phrases require a preposition and then -ing: think of moving, dream of travelling, succeed in completing, insist on paying and look forward to meeting. The to in look forward to is a preposition, not an infinitive marker.
explanation.example: They planned to move abroad but looked forward to visiting their old friends.

explanation.heading: An object can separate a verb and its pattern
explanation.body: Some verbs name a person or thing affected before the rest of the construction. Allow + object + to-infinitive describes permission; prevent + object + from + -ing describes something being stopped. Compare allowed the guests to enter with prevented the guests from entering. The presence of an object does not remove the required preposition.
explanation.example: The guard allowed visitors to wait inside but prevented them from entering the closed gallery.

comparisons.title: Fear of choosing an action versus fear of a consequence

left.label: Afraid to + verb
left.example: She was afraid to touch the painting.
left.note: She hesitated to act because touching it seemed risky.

right.label: Afraid of + -ing
right.example: She was afraid of damaging the painting.
right.note: She feared the possible consequence of touching it.

comparisons.title: Interest in an activity versus response to information

left.label: Interested in + -ing
left.example: We are interested in attending the lecture.

right.label: Interested to + verb
right.example: We were interested to learn about the findings.
right.note: Receiving the information caught our interest.

examples.sentence: The hikers were afraid of losing their way in the thick fog.
examples.note: The worry concerns a possible result: getting lost.

examples.sentence: I was afraid to ask for another extension.
examples.note: The speaker hesitated to perform the action.

examples.sentence: Are you interested in helping with the community garden?
examples.note: Interested in + -ing describes willingness to participate.

examples.sentence: I was sorry to hear that the concert was cancelled.
examples.note: Sorry to hear expresses regret about news.

examples.sentence: The manager prevented the visitors from taking photographs.

commonMistakes.incorrect: They are interested to joining the evening class.
commonMistakes.correct: They are interested in joining the evening class.
commonMistakes.why: Interest in participating takes interested in + -ing.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I am afraid to telling the truth to my manager.
commonMistakes.correct: I am afraid to tell the truth to my manager.
commonMistakes.why: The speaker is hesitant to take the action, so afraid to tell is the intended form.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I am sorry to shouting at you during the call.
commonMistakes.correct: I am sorry for shouting at you during the call.
commonMistakes.why: An apology for a past action normally uses sorry for + -ing.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The new rule prevented us to park near the entrance.
commonMistakes.correct: The new rule prevented us from parking near the entrance.
commonMistakes.why: Prevent + object requires from + -ing, not to-infinitive.

studyTips: Before choosing the verb form, decide whether the speaker fears taking an action or worries about a possible consequence.
Keep three short phrase families side by side: interested in doing / interested to hear; sorry for doing / sorry to hear; allowed to do / prevented from doing.
Underline the entire fixed phrase rather than only the word to: look forward to meeting and plan to meet have different grammatical patterns.

exercises.prompt: The cliff edge was narrow, so we walked slowly because we were afraid ___ our balance.
exercises.feedback: Afraid of losing describes the feared accidental outcome.

exercises.prompt: Leah wants to join the photography club. She is interested ___ a member.
exercises.feedback: Interested in + -ing expresses interest in participating.

exercises.prompt: I raised my voice in the meeting yesterday. I am sorry ___ so loudly.
exercises.feedback: Sorry for speaking apologises for an action already taken.

exercises.prompt: The safety barrier prevented visitors ___ the unfinished bridge.
exercises.feedback: Prevent + object + from + -ing is the required pattern.

exercises.prompt: The musician hesitated to take the stage. Complete with afraid to + the verb: She was afraid ___ in public. (perform)
exercises.feedback: Afraid to perform shows reluctance to take that action.

exercises.prompt: I am interested ___ more about the training programme. (in / learn)
exercises.feedback: Interested in learning describes interest in an activity.

exercises.prompt: I was interested ___ that the exhibition would open early. (hear)
exercises.feedback: Interested to hear expresses a reaction to receiving news.

exercises.prompt: They are looking forward ___ the new team next month. (to / meet)
exercises.feedback: Look forward to uses prepositional to followed by a gerund.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The children were afraid of fall into the stream.
acceptedAnswers: The children were afraid of falling into the stream.
exercises.feedback: Afraid of is followed by a gerund when a possible fall is feared.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I am sorry for hear about your broken bicycle.
acceptedAnswers: I am sorry to hear about your broken bicycle.
exercises.feedback: Sorry to hear expresses a sympathetic reaction to news.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: She insisted to pay for the tickets herself.
acceptedAnswers: She insisted on paying for the tickets herself.
exercises.feedback: Insist on + -ing is the standard pattern for insisting on an action.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The teacher allowed the students leaving the room early.
acceptedAnswers: The teacher allowed the students to leave the room early.

speakingExercises.prompt: The old ladder looks unstable. Say that Theo refuses to climb it because it feels dangerous. Begin “Theo is afraid” and end “the ladder”. Use afraid to.
acceptedAnswers: Theo is afraid to climb the ladder.
speakingExercises.feedback: Afraid to climb expresses hesitation about an action.

speakingExercises.prompt: The tiles are wet and there is a risk of slipping. Begin “We are afraid of” and use “slipping on the wet tiles”.
acceptedAnswers: We are afraid of slipping on the wet tiles.
speakingExercises.feedback: Afraid of slipping expresses fear of an unwanted outcome.

speakingExercises.prompt: You are considering volunteering at the shelter. Say one sentence beginning “I am interested in” and ending “at the shelter”. Use volunteer.
acceptedAnswers: I am interested in volunteering at the shelter.
speakingExercises.feedback: Interested in is followed by an -ing form.

speakingExercises.prompt: You have received surprising news about a promotion. Begin “I was interested to hear” and finish “about the promotion”.
acceptedAnswers: I was interested to hear about the promotion.
speakingExercises.feedback: Interested to hear expresses your reaction to new information.

speakingExercises.prompt: Apologise to a colleague for interrupting that colleague yesterday. Say exactly one sentence beginning “I am sorry for”, followed by “interrupting you yesterday”.
acceptedAnswers: I am sorry for interrupting you yesterday.
speakingExercises.feedback: Sorry for + -ing apologises for a completed action.

speakingExercises.prompt: You are about to ask a busy colleague a question. Use this exact polite phrase in a complete sentence: “I am sorry to bother you, but I have a question.”
acceptedAnswers: I am sorry to bother you, but I have a question.
speakingExercises.feedback: Sorry to bother you is a conventional polite apology while interrupting.

speakingExercises.prompt: Rephrase with prevent: “The rule stopped visitors from entering the garden.” Begin “The rule prevented” and keep “visitors” and “the garden”.
acceptedAnswers: The rule prevented visitors from entering the garden.
speakingExercises.feedback: Prevent + object + from + -ing names an action that was stopped.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences, using full forms. First: Maya / plan / apply / tomorrow. Second: she / look forward to / join / the team. Begin “Maya” and then “She”.
acceptedAnswers: Maya plans to apply tomorrow. She looks forward to joining the team.
speakingExercises.feedback: Plan takes a to-infinitive; look forward to takes a gerund.

listeningExercises.audioText: I wanted to climb the old tower, but I was afraid to use its narrow staircase.
choices: They had already climbed the tower.
They were not interested in the view.
listeningExercises.feedback: Afraid to use describes reluctance to take a particular action.

listeningExercises.audioText: The river was rising, and the campers were afraid of losing their tents in the flood.
listeningExercises.feedback: Afraid of losing points to a possible unwanted result.

listeningExercises.audioText: Our guests are interested in learning how the pottery is made.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word expression immediately after “interested” in the recording.
listeningExercises.feedback: Interested in learning describes willingness to explore an activity.

listeningExercises.audioText: I was interested to learn that the new library has a rooftop garden.
choices: Applying to work in the library.
A delay in the library opening.
listeningExercises.feedback: Interested to learn indicates the speaker found the news interesting.

listeningExercises.audioText: I am sorry for forgetting your birthday, and I will put a reminder in my calendar.
listeningExercises.prompt: What is the speaker apologising for?
choices: Arriving at a party too early.
listeningExercises.feedback: Sorry for forgetting is an apology for the past action.

listeningExercises.audioText: The caretaker allowed us to enter the courtyard but prevented us from going into the greenhouse.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which place could the visitors not enter?
listeningExercises.feedback: Prevented us from going into names the prohibited destination.

listeningExercises.audioText: The coach insisted on checking every bicycle before the race began.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word expression immediately after “insisted” in the recording.
listeningExercises.feedback: Insist on is followed by a gerund.

listeningExercises.audioText: I am looking forward to meeting the new project manager on Monday.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word expression immediately after “forward” in the recording.
listeningExercises.feedback: Looking forward to meeting includes the prepositional to and gerund meeting.
